question.prompt: When \(n\) standard six-sided dice are rolled, the product of the numbers rolled can be any of \(936\) possible values. What is \(n?\)

solutions.title: Count prime exponents
solutions.explanation:
Different rolls can have the same product, so count prime factorizations rather than arrangements of dice. Every possible product has a unique form \(2^h3^b5^c\), with nonnegative integer exponents.

Fix \(b\) and \(c\). Exactly \(b\) dice must show \(3\) or \(6\), and exactly \(c\) dice must show \(5\). Let
\[
d=n-b-c
\]
be the number of remaining dice, whose faces are \(1,2,4\).

The largest possible exponent \(h\) of \(2\) is \(b+2d\), obtained by choosing \(6\) for all \(b\) dice in the first group and \(4\) for all \(d\) dice in the last group. Every exponent down to \(0\) is possible: repeatedly change \(6\) to \(3\), or change \(4\) to \(2\) and then to \(1\). Each change removes exactly one factor of \(2\) while preserving \(b\) and \(c\). Thus this case contributes
\[
b+2d+1
\]
distinct products.

Let \(N(n)\) be the total number of products. We sum over all nonnegative triples \((b,c,d)\) satisfying \(b+c+d=n\):
\[
N(n)=\sum_{b+c+d=n}(b+2d+1).
\]
Swapping \(c\) and \(d\) leaves the collection of triples unchanged, so the sum of all \(d\)'s equals the sum of all \(c\)'s. Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
N(n)
&=\sum_{b+c+d=n}(b+c+d+1)\\
&=(n+1)\,\#\{(b,c,d):b+c+d=n\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
For \(b=0,1,\ldots,n\), the number of choices of \(c\) is respectively \(n+1,n,\ldots,1\), and \(d\) is then determined. Hence
\[
N(n)=(n+1)\frac{(n+1)(n+2)}2
=\frac{(n+1)^2(n+2)}2.
\]
This count has no duplication: distinct \((h,b,c)\) give distinct products by unique prime factorization, and every possible product was included.

At \(n=11\),
\[
N(11)=\frac{12^2\cdot13}{2}=936.
\]
The formula strictly increases for nonnegative integers \(n\), so this is the unique answer. Thus \(\boxed{n=11}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{A}}\).

solutions.title: Choose one representation per product
solutions.explanation:
The equalities \(1\cdot6=2\cdot3\), \(1\cdot4=2\cdot2\), and \(2\cdot6=3\cdot4\) let us simplify a collection of faces without changing either its product or its number of dice. We will use them to obtain representations that can be counted without duplication.

Starting with any roll, replace pairs \(1,6\) by \(2,3\) until no such pair remains. Next replace pairs \(1,4\) by \(2,2\) until none remain. Finally replace pairs \(2,6\) by \(3,4\) until none remain. If any \(1\)'s survived the first stage, there are no \(6\)'s, so the last stage cannot introduce a \(4\) alongside a surviving \(1\).

Consequently, the resulting faces belong to one of these three types. If a collection fits a type without its required face, assign it to the preceding type.

| Type | Allowed faces | Additional requirement | Number of multisets |
|---|---|---|---|
| I | \(1,2,3,5\) | None | \(\binom{n+3}{3}\) |
| II | \(2,3,4,5\) | At least one \(4\) | \(\binom{n+2}{3}\) |
| III | \(3,4,5,6\) | At least one \(6\) | \(\binom{n+2}{3}\) |

The first count distributes \(n\) identical dice among four face counts. Encoding those counts by \(n\) marks separated into four groups by three bars gives \(\binom{n+3}{3}\). In Type II, reserve one \(4\), then distribute the remaining \(n-1\) dice among four counts, giving \(\binom{n+2}{3}\). Reserving one \(6\) gives the same count for Type III.

We must check that these multisets represent distinct products. Write a product as \(2^h3^i5^j\), and let \(x_k\) denote the number of faces showing \(k\).

Within Type I, the exponents directly determine \(x_2,x_3,x_5\), and the remaining faces are \(1\)'s. Within Type II, \(x_3=i\) and \(x_5=j\); the equations
\[
x_2+x_4=n-i-j,\qquad x_2+2x_4=h
\]
determine the other counts. Within Type III, \(x_5=j\) and \(x_3+x_6=i\), so \(x_4=n-i-j\); then \(h=2x_4+x_6\) determines the remaining counts. Thus each type contains at most one representation of any product.

The types cannot overlap in product either:

* In Type I, \(h+i+j=n-x_1\le n\), which also implies \(h+2i+2j\le2n\).
* In Type II, \(h+i+j=n+x_4>n\), while \(h+2i+2j=2n-x_2\le2n\).
* In Type III, \(h+2i+2j=2n+x_6>2n\).

These inequalities distinguish all three types. The replacements prove that every obtainable product is represented, so the total is exactly
\[
\begin{aligned}
N(n)
&=\binom{n+3}{3}+2\binom{n+2}{3}\\
&=\frac{(n+1)(n+2)(n+3)+2n(n+1)(n+2)}6\\
&=\frac{(n+1)^2(n+2)}2.
\end{aligned}
\]
This strictly increasing expression equals \(936\) at \(n=11\), since \(12^2\cdot13/2=936\). Therefore \(\boxed{n=11}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{A}}\).
